A_baseline_without_rag.label: plausible_but_ungrounded
A_baseline_without_rag.text: Nikhilam is a clever Vedic trick near 100. You cross-subtract and multiply the gaps. It just works that way because ancient sages discovered it.

B_with_rag.label: retrieval_grounded
B_with_rag.text: Nikhilam works because of ordinary algebra. With base 100 and this app’s rule deviation = base − number, 98 and 97 are (100−2) and (100−3). Expanding gives 100×(100−2−3)+2×3 = 9506. The stage’s cross-subtraction and deviation product are that identity in disguise. Want to check what the deviation of 98 should be?

prompts.prompt: I don't understand why we carry 1 in Urdhva.

A_baseline_without_rag.label: handwavy
A_baseline_without_rag.text: You carry whenever the number looks big. Trust the animation arrow.

B_with_rag.label: retrieval_grounded
B_with_rag.text: A carry is place-value bookkeeping: when a column total is 10 or more, write the units digit and pass the tens to the next higher place. In Urdhva each sweep is one place-value column. I will not invent a carry digit—use the verified lesson column if we check this problem with tools.

prompts.prompt: Can you show me Anurupyena in the app?

A_baseline_without_rag.label: risk_of_fake_feature
A_baseline_without_rag.text: Sure—Anurupyena is ready. Watch the animation.

B_with_rag.label: boundary_grounded
B_with_rag.text: Anurupyena appears in some reference lists, but this app does not implement it as an interactive method. For general products here, use Urdhva; if both numbers are near a base, try Nikhilam.
